a.notes: Through the owner's lens the track series leads this heat, as the owner expected. The three new track entrants differ in page content (tables, timetables, readouts, figures, brackets), not in a corner wash, which is what the owner last asked for. Revival wins because it brings back the exact element the owner singled out as "one of the best design elements I've seen": the line round the page icon that brackets the head's controls, now on every page, with buffers and branches. Branch Lines is a very close second on figures drawn from each page's data. The ideal next round joins them: Revival's brackets, buffers and legend, Branch Lines' line from home and indication shelf, and Trued's one-line rows. Colour across all three is still grey-heavy slate and steel. The owner asked for subtle, tasteful companions so the page is not monochrome, and a measured period cyan on the 'to come' and plan marks is the best way to answer that without going warm. Glow: every track entrant keeps a real halo on the mark, the key word, the lamps and the tubes, with the rest matte, which is right. Grafts that worked: the line from home on Ideas (a figure from data, lit as phosphor); the Status indication shelf with counts; figures in the page heads; the departure board listing the next plans (timetable-graft); the four-week pulse trace (pocket-graft); setup folded to one step with a count (timetable-graft); Settings as a lamp list. Grafts that did not work: the double-track chat, busy in Branch Lines but fine as a meridian in Night Departures; numbered lines in the bar ('1 Vera 2 Ideas'), which are noise; a week track on the month that only shows on the last row; spines coloured per section. Across the Night Timetable line, warm companions (copper names, yellow links, earlier the hazard stripe and arrow tiles) stand beside the green rather than supporting it, which is the owner's standing objection to warm browns and tans. The Pocket line's thick rounded lens cases and pixel titles repeat the owner's 'case too dominant' note, and the Instruments mutant makes that worse. Yardsticks: today's page 3.5 (bright monochrome, old title); Desk Terminal, Joined 7.2 (grounded and well built, but little line art and the old title lit in its tube).

scores.why: The owner's own favourite element is back on every page: the line rings each page icon, drops, turns one 45-degree chamfer and runs under the head's controls (Ideas, Plans, To do). Around it are buffer stops, a branch for 'If that one cannot', a lamp legend, the setup steps as a vertical line and 'your turn' at the chat box, which together make the signal-box language the owner called 'high style'. Slate and steel are grounded, the tube light is on the lit 'line', the lamps and the monitors, and the big condensed title gives Home a real voice. It loses points for Status' empty Keys board and slightly grey-heavy colour.

Passes the owner's latest test best: the changes are the page content itself. Ideas gets a glowing 'line from home' built from its own data, Status an indication shelf with '6 working, 7 off', the page heads carry figures (Ideas 12) and the Plans list reads as a timetable, all in the track language with ringed page icons. Held back by being very green-and-grey (90% green share; Chat and Status read monochrome) and by a double-track chat that reads busy.

The cleanest system: one-line rows under proper column heads on slate, a real To do timetable with a lit now, a spend readout on Status, Settings as a lamp list and three lines on Home. It is calm and grounded, with the glow only on live things. But the greeting's type is small next to its siblings, and the page-head line stops short of bracketing the controls.

The spine leaves each page's tile and plugs sections in at square nodes, which is fine structural line art the owner likes. The Next up tube draws four weeks as glowing pulses, content lit as phosphor, and To do is cut by a lit NOW line. Condensed heads give a good type step. The graphite lens cases are still thick and rounded, and colouring the To do spine lemon muddies the one-meaning colours.

A strong idea well realised: the tube is a real departure board of the next four plans, the question is the first stop on Vera's line, and 'Finish setting up' folds to one step with a count. The owner reads warm tan as off-motif, and copper family names beside wayfinding-yellow links pull warm against the green. The line numbers in the bar ('1 Vera 2 Ideas') are noise.

NOW, NEXT and LATER on a steel spine is a clear, friendly structure, and the costume is mostly gone. The pixel display face on page titles fights the sans heads. Amber and lemon links, pink kids and thick graphite lens cases keep it busier and warmer than the owner likes.

The costume is gone and the good structure is kept: Vera's line down the centre of Home, a portrait radar beside an Ideas table, and a To do timetable. Copper names, yellow links, enamel leads under heads and tiny superscript numbers in the bar are still noise that does not support the green.

Track Diagram with the lit run from now and the glow put back. It is on-motif and calm, but the page structure is the same as its parent, and it keeps the boxed To do cards, the Ideas card grid and 'What's on your mind?'.

The machine lights and the family stays matte, a good rule, and the lit now stops and lamp legends are nice. Otherwise the parent's layout is almost untouched and the title keeps the old words, so it looks like its parent with the lights turned up.

The owner's round-10 favourite still has the right language (fortnight track, To do timetable margin, chat hung from Vera). Beside its own descendants it now reads unfinished: card grids, boxed To do rows, dimmer glow and the old title.
The time spine is the right idea, but the pixel type, the olive-green wash, the pink NOW and the heavy pewter handheld cases make it the monochrome costume the owner asked to calm.

A good station-line structure buried under costume: a hazard stripe, rainbow numbered discs, yellow arrow tiles and copper bubbles. That is colour beside the green rather than supporting it, and 33 small targets on Home.
Only the type moved. Workbench on the tubes is heavy and its slashed zeros are hard to read, and every fault of the parent's costume stays.

The drawn scopes with knobs, jacks and speakers are charming but pure costume, and they make the cases heavier and more dominant, the opposite of the owner's note about thick bezels. Nothing without a screen changes.

Grounded slate trays, amber held for late and setup, and a lit green terminal on every page (radar, gauge, bar chart) keep the CRT soul spread across the whole page. Bright green appears only where it means something, and there are thin tracks with a NOW stop in Coming up, To do and chat. It scores below the track series because the steel-blue selected chips take the green's signature job and read as more blue than needed, the line art is lighter than Signal Box's, and it keeps 'What's on your mind?'.

The real glow, scanlines and radar are the DNA the owner wants kept. But this is the page the owner asked to change: a green haze across the hero, bright high-contrast mint everywhere, thick rounded cards, a brown-bordered tan setup box and pink names. It has none of the line art and none of the grounded supporting colour, and its title is the generic 'What's on your mind?'.

fixes.suggestion: Keep: the head bracket (ring, drop, 45-degree chamfer, run under the controls) on every page; buffer stops at the ends of lines; 'If that one cannot' as a branch; the lamp legend; setup as a vertical line; 'your turn' at the chat box; the big condensed greeting; one-line Ideas rows with DRIVE and WAY columns. Fix: Status' Keys and Connected boards are stretched to Who answers' height, so let each board size to its content, or drop the three boards and hang them on one line. Fill the dead band beside the spend tube with Branch Lines' indication shelf (lamps banked by group, with '6 working, 7 off'). Take Branch Lines' 'line from home' onto Ideas, inside the head's bracket above the table, instead of the tall portrait radar. Put a head figure beside Ideas, To do and Plans. Colour is almost all slate and steel: give 'to come' rings and the Coming up plates a measured period cyan cap so the page is not grey-green alone. Make the fortnight's rail end at its last stop's buffer. Title: set 'What shall we plan?' or 'What's the plan?' at this display size, with the job word lit.

Keep: the glowing 'line from home' on Ideas, the Status indication shelf with its counts, the figures in the page heads, the week track on the month, the Plans list as a timetable, and the Settings lamp list. Fix: Plans' head says '1 plan in September' when three plans are coming. Count what is coming ('3 coming, next tomorrow'). The Ideas line spends a quarter of the glass on 0 to 18 minutes with no station: start the axis at a break, or at the nearest place. Chat's double rail with times under each stop is busy: keep one rail with times in the margin, and keep the 'Sun 27 Sep' plate. Chat and Status are nearly all green and grey, so give the family's initials and their bubble bar steel-cyan and the lamps their one-meaning colours. Add Revival's chamfered bracket so the head line holds 'Save a thought', List/Month and Show.

Keep: one-line rows under column heads everywhere, To do as a timetable (DUE in the margin, lamps, a lit now), the Status spend readout, Settings as a lamp list, and the 'now' lamp and run on Home's fortnight. Fix: the greeting 'What's the plan?' is set too small for Home's first line, so step it up to Revival's condensed display size. Let the page-head line bracket the controls (Open/Done/Cancelled/All, List/Month) rather than stopping under the lede. On Home, give the kids' wishes a compact line rather than a fourth tray of empty rows.

Keep: the spine leaving each page tile and plugging sections in at square nodes, the NOW and NEXT plates, the four-week pulse trace in Next up, To do cut by a lit NOW line, Status sections as nodes, and the condensed heads. Fix: thin the graphite lens cases to a 2 to 3px bezel with small radii. Keep every spine steel, with the section colour only on the tile and cap (the lemon To do spine blurs amber's one job). Shorten To do's wide 'Edit, complete, or snooze' buttons to 'Edit'. Centre Chat's day stop on the spine on the phone.

Keep: the departure board listing the next four plans with dotted leaders, the question as the first lit stop on Vera's line, the setup folded to one step with a '3', and the chat meridian. Fix: copper names reads as warm tan beside amber 'was due', so move the family's names and initials to steel or bone. Make links steel-denim, underlined, not wayfinding yellow. Drop the numbers from the bar's links. Make To do's rows one line (task, who, due, Edit) instead of three. Give the page heads a line that brackets their controls.

Keep: the three columns of Home with Vera's line in the middle, the portrait radar beside the Ideas table, and the To do timetable with NOW. Fix: the superscript numbers on the bar's icons look like notification badges, so remove them. Replace the copper names and yellow links with steel. Use one length of enamel lead under heads, not two.

Keep: NOW, NEXT and LATER with the dotted run-on and the one-line Coming up rows. Fix: drop the pixel face from the page titles and use the condensed heads Traced uses. Thin the lens cases. Keep amber for late only (the setup tray's links and step numbers are amber, and 'All 4' is lemon).

a.titles: Best: "What's the plan?" (t1-track-refine, t1-timetable-refine, t1-pocket-refine). It is the family's own kitchen-table phrase, it asks for exactly what FamilyDB keeps, and the lit word is the job itself. It is short enough to hold one line on any phone. Its only cost is a slight echo of the placeholder's "Plans for the weekend". Close second: "What's next for us?" (t1-track-graft, t1-timetable-graft, t1-pocket-graft). It speaks as a household ("us"), leans forward in time and is a warm invitation, but "next" says schedule more than ideas or wishes, and the lit word is less the job than "plan". "What shall we line up?" (t1-track-revival) is clever and set beautifully large. But "shall" is a little stiff, and the lit word names the lineage's motif, not the family's job, so it reads as a pun. The fix is "What shall we plan?" with "plan" lit, which keeps the "we" and the job word at Revival's display size. Fails: "What's on your mind?", kept by r10-idea-3, r13-mut-4, r10-wild-3, r11-wild-1, the three dice mutants and both yardsticks (lit inside Desk Terminal's tube). It is a generic chat opener that says nothing of weekends, plans, reminders or wishes.

a.notes:
The three strongest designs this round, one per lineage, each made a tube carry the page's own data (line from home, departure board, pulse trace). That is exactly the owner's 'reflect more of the page content' done in light, and it is how the original's soul comes back without glare.

Grafts that worked:
- The Status indication shelf (track-graft): glowing dots on the black.
- The Ideas drive-time strip chart (track-graft): a real period tube carrying data.
- The departure-board rows with dotted leaders (timetable-graft).
- The Plans head's figures (timetable-graft).
- The NOW line cutting To do (pocket-graft and all three track entrants).
- The pulse trace of the coming weeks (pocket-graft).
- The lit newest stop in Chat (timetable-graft).

Grafts that did not:
- The meridian two-sided chat now appears in three lineages (track-graft, timetable-graft, pocket-graft). It works, but the lineages are converging on it; keep each lineage's own chat voice (the track's merge into one lit line is the most its own).
- Pocket-graft's chamfered cartridges and amber afterglow.
- Pocket-graft folding Memory, Family and Status into the phone's Settings key.
- The shelf's floating box on Status, which leaves dead slate.

Afterglow is the kit effect most often lost this round. In the track entrants' details strips the row afterglow is nearly invisible; only track-mut shows a clear green fade. Every lineage's standard should state it: a phosphor or sage edge, 1.2s, visible at 120ms. Power-on and focus are faithful in all sixteen.

The dice mutants taught one thing each:
- track-mut: 'the machine lights, the family is matte' is worth grafting as a rule, minus the glowing page head.
- timetable-mut: a heavier CRT face adds weight, not light.
- pocket-mut: drawn hardware is costume.

The carried originals r11-wild-1 and pocket-mut show the failure mode clearly: a green-tinted page is glare, not glow.

scores.why: This is where the soul comes from: full halos, the greeting's pool, a real radar tube and breathing lamps. But the glow is spread over every greeting border, pill and card edge, so it is glare more than scarcity (the 'Matrix' complaint), and the tubes only decorate.

The question sits on the tube itself in VT323 with a lit cursor, every page has a tube that carries its own data (gauge, To do bars), and the glow elsewhere is scarce. A strong benchmark for light and meaning; the page around it is a little flat.
A good lamp-and-line language, but the tube is dulled (screen #74f0a3, screenGlow 0.8, glow 0.9). The monitors read dimmer than today's and the lamps are flat dots, not light.

Full glow is back and there is a lit 'now' lamp on To do, which helps, but the rest is the parent's page: the tubes are unchanged, row afterglow is barely visible, and there is no new place where the light means something.

The light is disciplined. The lit 'now' lamp trails a short lit run to the first stop, the greeting has its pool, 'plan' has a real halo, Status gets a spend tube and a lamp legend, and everything else is matte slate. Calm and correct, but the lit key word is small, the row afterglow is a 12% steel wash that barely shows, and the phone bar is broken.

The best lit key word here: a big condensed 'What shall we line up?' with 'line' blooming in a two-layer halo over the original greeting pool. The lamp legend (live, to come, done, late, off, stopped) runs from Status to Settings, 'your turn' is lit at the chat's terminus, and the fallback on Status is a turnout ending at a buffer. Light where something is live, and a system behind it.

Each page gets a phosphor instrument drawn from its own data: Ideas' 'THE LINE FROM HOME' is a real green-screen strip chart of drive times, Status' indication shelf is glowing dots on the black, the month has a lit run from today, and Chat's two rails merge into one lit line into the box. This is the owner's 'reflect the page content' done in light, though Chat and Status lean almost only green.

'The machine lights, the family is matte' is a real phosphor rule: her times are lit readouts, her bubbles get a green glass edge, the Now readout sits on To do, and the afterglow is a visible green fade. But the big glowing 'Vera' page head and the lit date on Home spread the glow past scarcity, and the tubes and structure are still the parent's.
The dot-matrix Next up board is a lovely period tube, but glow is cut to 0.7/0.9/0.5, the greeting has no pool, and the hazard stripe and yellow arrow tiles are costume standing in for light.

Full tube light is back: a bright NEXT UP board, a glass pool rising from her line through the box, a haloed 'plan', a lit newest stop in chat, and a spend tube on Status. The top-left board and Ideas' tall, fully lit portrait radar outshine the box, and the superscript numbers in the bar add noise.

The departure board is the most convincing 1980s green screen in the heat. It lists the next plans with times and dotted leaders, so the tube carries the page's content, not decoration. Beside it are a green-glass ask box, a lit 'Continue with Vera' terminus, and the newest chat stop with her screen and time aglow. The yellow links and the loud amber '3' spend some of the scarcity.

Workbench on the tubes is raster-lit and properly CRT, but it is heavy, and its slashed zero misreads ('10 places' looks like '18'). It keeps the parent's dimmed glow numbers, so the light is louder in weight, not better in meaning.
Green tints the whole ground and every card border, and Silkscreen headings are everywhere. Phosphor is a wash across the page, the opposite of scarce light, and the tubes are lost in it.

The page is calmer now: a lit NOW plate, a hollow breathing NEXT, a haloed 'plan', labelled tubes and a month tube on Plans, with slate everywhere else. The Silkscreen page titles read as handheld costume more than tube light, and the NEXT row is sparse.

Time is drawn in light: lit NOW and NEXT plates, a lit spine between them, a square-pulse scope trace of the next four weeks on the Next up tube, the month tube's pulses, a lit NOW line cutting To do, and NOW as the chat box's tab. Calm slate around it. The afterglow is amber (a kind colour), not phosphor, and the chamfered cartridges are costume.

The drawn scopes are charming period hardware, but the knobs, jacks and speakers tell the family nothing. The page keeps the parent's green wash and pixel type, so the light is everywhere and the tubes grow heavier, not brighter.

fixes.suggestion: KEEP: Ideas' 'THE LINE FROM HOME' strip-chart tube, Status' indication shelf of glowing lamps, the month's week track with its lit run from today, Chat's rails merging into one lit line into the box, and the lamp at each Settings row. FIX: (1) Home is still the parent's greeting. Take the revival's large condensed title with its lit word and the revival's lamp legend, so Home has the same lit-instrument weight as Ideas and Status. (2) On Status the shelf floats in a slate box with dead space under it. Put the spend tube and the shelf behind one bezel as a single lit instrument panel, and make each lamp group head the board below it. (3) Row afterglow is a 12% steel wash that no still shows. Make it a sage/phosphor edge fading over the kit's 1.2s afterglow curve, visible at 120ms. (4) In Chat, light only the newest stop (her screen and time, as Night Departures does) and leave the older bubbles' edges matte, so the light marks now. (5) On the Ideas tube, stack the station numbers on two fixed baselines and keep the lit run only as far as the nearest place, so the 'home' end of the glass doesn't read empty.

KEEP: the big condensed 'What shall we line up?' with 'line' in the full two-layer halo over the original greeting pool; the LAMPS legend as a site-wide standard; the turnout and buffer stop for 'If that one cannot'; 'your turn' lit at the chat's terminus; the spend tube top-right on Status. FIX: at rest the chat's message box is matte while its lamp is lit. Give it Home's faint resting glow so the terminus and the box read as one lit stop. Row afterglow is invisible (see track-graft). On Status, Keys and Connected to are stretched to Who answers' height, leaving empty slate; top-align them. The Ideas portrait radar is the brightest block on the page, so cap its height to the list's first eight rows.

Graft its rule, not the page: the machine's times and the newest of her lines as lit readouts, the family matte. Drop the halo from the big 'Vera' page head and from Home's date: a lit heading at 2.5rem is glare. Keep the white-hot lamp cores and the visible green afterglow on her rows; those belong in the track standard.

KEEP: the departure board (NEXT UP, then the next plans as 'Sun 13:00 Oaks Park roller rink ...... in 4 days' with a '1 more' link), the green-glass ask box with its phosphor edge, the lit 'Continue with Vera' terminus, the newest chat stop lit, and the Plans head's figures ('1 plan in September, next up tomorrow at 10:00'). FIX: (1) Wayfinding yellow on every Home link (All plans, All wishes, Maya, Theo, Continue with Vera) competes with the lit terminus. Make links steel and keep yellow for nothing, or for the terminus alone. (2) The Send key renders pale mint. Set it to exact #6dff9c with the kit's ring and pool, so the one primary is the brightest green. (3) The huge amber '3' beside 'Finish setting up' is the loudest mark on Home. Set it at label size. (4) Put the board on her line as the stop after the box, the way Pocket puts NEXT under NOW, so the lit board and the lit box read as one line rather than two rival columns. (5) Drop or shrink the bar's line numbers ('1 Vera 2 Ideas'); they are costume, not light.

Keep the glass pool rising from her line through the box, and the lit newest chat stop. Shrink the top-left NEXT UP board or move it onto the line so the box, not the board, is the brightest thing. Replace the superscript numbers on the bar icons. Cap the Ideas portrait radar's height.

KEEP: the lit NOW and NEXT plates with the lit spine between them, the square-pulse scope trace of the next four weeks on the Next up tube, the month tube's pulses on Plans, the lit NOW line through To do, and NOW as the chat box's tab. FIX: (1) Row afterglow is amber from the kind colour. Make it a phosphor/sage edge fading over 1.2s: amber is 'late' and nothing else. (2) The chamfered cartridge cards in Lately added are handheld costume; use the one-line rows the other pages use. (3) The trace's day numbers are 10px; set them at label size and light only the next pulse's number. (4) On the phone, don't fold Memory, Family and Status into 'Settings'. (5) Status lights only Who answers' node; give every live row its breathing lamp as on Home.

Keep the NOW plate and the calmer slate. Replace the Silkscreen page titles with the bone condensed heads pocket-graft uses: pixel type reads as a Game Boy, not a tube. Fill NEXT's sparse label row with the trace from pocket-graft.

a.titles: Best: 'What's next for us?' (t1-timetable-graft, t1-pocket-graft, t1-track-graft) and 'What's the plan?' (t1-track-refine, t1-timetable-refine, t1-pocket-refine). Through this lens 'next' wins wherever a NEXT tube sits below it. The lit word and the tube's NEXT UP become one voice, so the glow means something: in Night Departures the board answers the question, and in Pocket Traced the lit NEXT plate sits directly under 'next'. The family's 'us' also makes it a household question, not one person's. Its weakness is that an idea to keep or a reminder isn't quite 'next'. 'What's the plan?' is the most job-true and shortest, and 'plan' names what FamilyDB keeps, but it echoes the placeholder's 'Plans for the weekend' just below. 'What shall we line up?' (revival) has the best-lit word typographically: large, condensed, with the full halo. 'Line' is the page's own motif, which suits a page drawn in lines. But 'shall' is a little formal, and 'line up' can read as a queue; 'What shall we line up next?' would carry both. Fails: 'What's on your mind?', kept by the mutants and the carried designs. It is generic and says nothing of planning, and 'mind' lights a word that belongs to no tube.

a.notes:
The owner's test ('reflect more of the page content') separates this heat cleanly. The winners are those whose glass carries the family's data:
- the departure board with leaders (timetable-graft)
- the 4-week pulse trace and the month pulses (pocket-graft)
- the line from home and the indication shelf (track-graft)

The refinements are tidier but mostly look like their parents at thumbnail size.

Grafted features that worked:
- The departure-board list of the next plans. It is the best graft in the heat, and phosphor with a job.
- The pulse trace on the tube.
- The Vera meridian chat. It landed in both track-graft and timetable-graft and suits both, though Timetable's warm copper version is more inviting than Track's steel double rail.
- The one-step setup card with its big amber count (timetable-graft).
- Head counts and ledes ('1 plan in September · next up tomorrow at 10:00'; 'Ideas 12, 10 on the line').
- The '6 working · 7 off' Status figure.

Grafts that did not work as well:
- Pocket-graft's chamfered Lately added cartridges, a second visual language.
- Track-graft's Ideas line, where the tick numbers cluster.
- The heavy boxed 'Edit, complete, or snooze' buttons.

A caution for round 2: the grafts are converging. All three lineages now have a meridian or axis chat, a NOW rule in To do, condensed titles and steel on slate. Each lineage should keep its own dialect, or the finals will look alike:
- Track: steel rails, buffers, lamps, 45-degree turns.
- Timetable: warm ink, enamel leads, yellow wayfinding, departures on leaders.
- Pocket: square stops, lit NOW/NEXT plates, pulses.

On the dice mutants:
- The type roll (Workbench on the tube) found the heat's most memorable letterforms and should be grafted in narrowly.
- The graphics roll (the drawn scope) is lovely illustration but costume.
- The phosphor roll on Track changed only the halo.

Grounded colour: Timetable handles it best, with warm ink and copper people. Track still reads as one cold blue-grey.

Yardsticks: timetable-graft and pocket-graft now beat Desk Terminal, Joined on mood and on content in light.

scores.why: Yardstick. Recognisably Phosphor and lit well on its two tubes, but everything else is stock dark-mode cards, and the green is everywhere. The family's "Matrix" remark still holds.

Yardstick. A coherent, considered system: the terminal side panel with its gauge, numbered sections and tabular mono. It is calm and grown-up, though a little office-like. This heat's best entrants now match or beat it on mood and on graphics drawn from the data.

The mimic-line idea is fresh on Home: the fortnight line and the To do line with its lamps. But every row is still a raised plate, Ideas and Status are the old card grids, and the steel-on-slate mood is cool to the point of anonymous.
The same design with the lamps and the now-run lit. The light lands where it should and lifts it a little, but the structure and the plate-on-plate texture are unchanged.

Better typeset: Ideas and Status became real one-line tables, the portrait radar sits beside Ideas, the spend tube leads Status, and there is a lamp legend. At a glance, though, Home is the parent's, and the folded phone bar is cramped. Tidier rather than more distinctive.

It has the most railway character in the series: 45-degree chamfers, T buffer stops, a vertical setup line, and a small 'your turn' where the chat line meets the box. The bold 40px greeting is the best headline in the lineage. The layout is still the parent's, and the slate-and-steel palette alone reads as a costume of grey.

The most page content changed in this lineage. Ideas has a lit glass figure ('the line from home' on a log scale), Status an indication shelf of lamps with a big '6 working · 7 off', and Chat a double-track meridian. This finally answers the owner's 'reflect more of the page content'. Home is still the parent's, and the page is nearly all steel and green (90% green share).

The lit machine voice on the lamps and Vera's times is right in principle, but the dice changed light, not form. It reads as the parent with a brighter halo, and the frozen 'Wed 00:22' readout feels like a bug.

A real personality: a station at night, with enamel line numbers, Vera's line down Home and a dot-matrix board. The costume is loud, though: a hazard stripe, yellow arrow tiles, copper-brown family bubbles and enamel discs everywhere.

The costume is gone and the mood kept: warm-white ink, wayfinding-yellow links, a short enamel rule under each sign, the board top-left, her line down the middle, and a To do timetable with NOW in the margin. Grounded and distinctive. Faults: fussy superscript numbers on the nav icons, and copper owners beside amber late words.

The one the family would call lovely. The Next up screen is a real departure board listing the next plans on dotted leaders, which is phosphor carrying content. Home is a balanced three-column station, Chat splits along Vera's meridian, the Plans lede reads '1 plan in September · next up tomorrow at 10:00', and a wide display face gives the titles a voice of their own. The light sits only on what is live.

Workbench's raster on the Next up tube ('Silver Falls hike' with its drawn bleed) is the most memorable piece of type in the heat. Everything outside the glass is the untouched parent: hazard stripe, arrow tiles, discs.

Charming and brave, with a handheld spine, NOW/NEXT/LATER and pixel stops. But the pixel face on titles and item names, the olive tint and the chunky pixel borders make it a toy costume that tires quickly and reads poorly.

The spine is kept and the costume dropped: square stops (filled for places, hollow for to-come, dashed for LATER), a lit NOW with the date, a To do list with NOW and SOMEDAY cuts, and a month tube beside the agenda. A friendly, clear system. It keeps a pixel face for page titles, which fights the condensed sans of the greeting.

Time drawn in light. The NEXT tube traces the next four weeks as square pulses, and the month tube pulses under each planned day. NOW and NEXT are lit plates on the spine, To do is a due queue cut by a lit NOW rule, and Chat ends in the lit box with NOW as its tab. The condensed titles and bone heads make one coherent voice. Only the boxed right column on Home is generic.

The drawn pocket scope, with its handle, knobs, speaker grille and lamp, is genuinely delightful illustration. But it is costume that says nothing about the family's data, its smooth shading clashes with the pixel page, and it makes Home heavier.

fixes.suggestion: KEEP: the departure-board Next up (the next plans on dotted leaders with 'in 4 days'), Vera's line down Home ending at 'Continue with Vera', the one-step setup card with its big amber '3', the inline numbered bar ('1 Vera 2 Ideas'), the Chat meridian, the Plans lede with its counts, the To do timetable with the NOW rule, the wide display face, and warm ink with copper family names. a.notes: What worked across the heat is the owner's latest test: the designs that moved furthest from today's page did it by drawing each page's own data. Those are the pulse trace (pocket-graft), the departures list (timetable-graft), the line from home and the indication shelf (track-graft), and the Plans agenda with the month on glass (Pocket). Each lineage's graft beat its refinement, because the grafts changed content and the refinements mostly cleaned up. Grafted features that worked: figure-led page heads from Figure Ground ('Ideas 12', '4 open · 2 late') on track-graft; the double-track meridian chat on track-graft, which is better than Night Timetable's own; an annunciator-style indication shelf on Status (track-graft); a flight-plan pulse trace on the NEXT tube (pocket-graft); a departure-board listing on the tube and a collapsed setup with a count (timetable-graft); and hairline heads that run to their links (pocket-graft). Keep it and give the question the top rank. (2) The 'here' state should be a latched slate cell with a steel cap, never a bright fill. (3) Amber must mean only late: kind words and restaurant rings keep leaking it. (4) Controls are near-identical across the field (green double focus ring, slate selects with a tick or dot, sage tick). All are fine; the choice between them is not decisive. a.titles: The strongest two titles, through the page's type system: "What's the plan?" (track-refine, timetable-refine, pocket-refine) and "What's next for us?" (track-graft, timetable-graft, pocket-graft). "What's the plan?" is the tightest (16 characters, one line on any phone at 40px). It is the family's own phrase, and its lit word names the job itself, so it works at display size as the page's top-ranked head. Its one flaw is the echo of 'Plans for the weekend' in the placeholder, which is minor because the placeholder reads as the answers. "What's next for us?" is warmer (a household 'us'). It fits the time-ordered lineages best, because the lit 'next' rhymes with the NEXT stop, the NEXT UP board and the departures, so the question and the page speak one word. Its scope is a little narrower (an idea to keep is not quite 'next'). I would give "What's next for us?" to Pocket and Night Timetable, and "What's the plan?" to the track series. "What shall we line up?" (revival) fails by comparison: the glow goes on a motif word ('line') rather than a job word, and 'shall we' is formal for a family kitchen. The carried designs and the mutants keep "What's on your mind?", which says nothing about planning and which the owner has rejected. Placement matters as much as wording: the question must be the largest head on Home. Refine sets it at about 22px, under 24px section heads, which undoes any title.

a.notes:
THROUGH THIS LENS:
- The Pocket spine wins because time runs down the page in the order a family asks: what now, what next, what later. It survives the squint better than any other structure here.
- The refinements did the most for usability. All four fixed the small targets (0 or 1 under 44px against today's 43 of 56), and turned To do's select into keys. They also replaced the per-card disclosure with one-line rows and a labelled Edit, and put counts such as '4 open · 2 late' in the head.
- Keyboard: the Tab order after the bar is the textarea, then who is asking, Send and the ways to start in every design, so it matches the one action. On the three-column Timetable Homes the tube and Coming up come first visually but after the box in the Tab order, which is acceptable because the box is the one action.
- Focus rings are the same strong double green ring in all designs, and the details strips show no regression.

GRAFTS THAT WORKED:
- Timetable graft: the departure board (four plans on one tube) and the one-step setup card.
- Pocket graft: the four-week pulse trace, and the full-width dashed NOW on To do.
- Track graft: the double-track Chat, and the idea count in the Ideas head.
- Revival: the buffer-stop links ('All plans' at the end of the line) and the vertical setup line with the next step lit.

GRAFTS THAT DID NOT:
- Track graft: the Status indication shelf (unlabelled lamps, and '7 off' counts keys nobody needs as faults), and the week track under the month.
- Pocket graft: a second add field on To do, a heavy 'Edit, complete, or snooze' button on every row, scope jargon ('1 WK/DIV'), and the phone Settings key hiding Memory, Family and Status.
- Timetable lineage: the line numerals in the bar and the section heads read as counts.

MUTANTS:
- Pocket mutant: the drawn knobs are false affordances.
- Timetable mutant: Workbench makes the tube harder to read.
- Track mutant: its lit 'Now' clock stop is a good cue but goes stale.

AGAINST THE OWNER'S TEST (the change must reach page content):
- Pocket-refine and pocket-graft reshape Home, Plans, To do and Chat.
- Track-refine and track-revival reshape To do, Ideas, Status and Settings.
- Timetable-graft reshapes Home.
- The dice mutants barely change how anything is used.

Yardstick. Every page has the same left console (monitor, then its controls as large keys) and numbered tables on the right, with 0 small targets. The tube holds the question, so the brightest thing is also the first stop. Two small costs: the tube's two links come before the textarea in the Tab order, and the question is set in mono inside the glass.

The lines work where there is an order: the fortnight, To do's due timetable, the setup steps. Only one target is small. But the question is set small, To do still hides each action in a disclosure behind a Show select, and Ideas and Status are still plates in boxes.
The parent plus a lit 'now' lamp on To do's line, which helps the reader place 'late' against 'coming'. Nothing else about how the page is used changes.

The parent's layout with lit readouts. The 'Now Wed 00:22' stop is a nice cue, though it goes stale, and 'late' is said in words. To do keeps the select and the disclosure cards, so how the page is used is unchanged.

The hazard-striped setup banner sits above the question and takes the eye first. Numbered coloured discs in the bar and yellow arrow tiles compete, and 33 of 57 Home targets are under 44px. The line from the question through the ways to start is a good idea buried in noise.

Much calmer than its parent. The best single-screen Home in the heat: the departure board lists the next four plans on leaders, and setup shrinks to one next step plus 'All 3 steps'. But the line numbers read as counts ('2 Ideas' in the bar beside 'All 12 ideas'), Home's section numbers run 3, 5, 4, 2 out of reading order, the board outshines the question in the squint, and To do still repeats 'No active reminder' and a disclosure on every row.

The heavy raster of Workbench makes the tube text (the plan's name, '10 places from home', times with slashed zeros) harder to read, and it keeps all the parent's faults, including 33 small Home targets and the hazard banner first.

The NOW, NEXT, Coming up, LATER spine is the right order for Home. But a pixel display face on item names and headings slows reading, and the handheld costume and 25 small targets on To do cost usability.

The clearest page in the heat to read and use. Blurred, it still runs NOW, the big 'What's the plan?' with its lit Send, then NEXT's tube, Coming up ('4 more after Next up', so nothing is repeated), then LATER. To do opens with a green primary add, then the keys, '4 open, 2 late', NOW and SOMEDAY stops and a labelled Edit. Plans lists only the days that hold something, with today marked, beside a month tube, and every target is 44px or more. Its costs are the pixel face on page titles and 72px Coming up rows that are mostly empty.

It keeps pocket-refine's sight line and adds real information: the four-week trace in Next up shows how busy the month is at a glance, and To do gets a dashed NOW line across the list, with 0 small targets. It is muddied by two ways to add on To do (the primary button plus a 'What needs doing' field), a heavy 'Edit, complete, or snooze' button on every row, scope jargon ('1 WK/DIV'), and Memory, Family and Status hidden inside a Settings key on the phone.

a.notes:
Through the typesetting lens the track series is ahead this round. All three new track entrants have a real type system:
- Condensed Archivo titles with tight tracking over DM Sans.
- DM Mono kept for figures and times.
- Margin timetables whose figures right-align.

They differ in the tables:
- The revival's separate DRIVE and WAY columns are the most exact.
- The graft's figures beside titles give numbers a job at the top of each page.
- The refine's stated token scale (17px body) is the one to adopt for the whole app.

A merged track design is the one to aim for: the refine's scale, the revival's tables and Settings list, and the graft's title figures and sentence-case heads.

Grafted features that worked:
- Figures beside the titles, and Status's '6 working · 7 off' counts (track-graft).
- The departure board with dot leaders and the inline nav numerals (timetable-graft).
- Plex Mono date kickers over bold titles in the Plans list (pocket-graft).

Grafted features that did not work:
- Track-graft's centred chat meridian with a right-set 'Vera' title, and its line-from-home station labels, which collide.
- Pocket-graft's cartridges on Home, which break names mid-phrase.
- Timetable-graft's three-line To do rows.

The phosphor mutants show that lighting body text (track-mut's lit mint words for Vera) costs crispness. Keep the halo on marks, the key word and the tube faces, never on sentences.

The type mutant proves a CRT face on the glass can carry character, but only with an open zero and at display sizes.

Across the heat, the main typographic debt is Home's row text at 12-13px: every lineage should set Home's lists at the body step.

Recurring small faults still to purge:
- Tracked mono caps dates ('WEDNESDAY 30 SEPTEMBER').
- A date broken from its time on the Next up tube.
- Direction glued to durations, so 'min' cannot align.

scores.why: Yardstick. DM Sans and DM Mono do their jobs, but the heads are timid, the small labels are tracked mono caps, the lists have no tabulation, and Home's type is all about one size. Readable, but there is barely a type scale.

Yardstick. Right-aligned tabular mono figures in real columns (Coming up, To do, Status 'n of m'), numbered section heads, and figures that line up everywhere. Held back by very small Home and Status type and by mono used for sentences (her words, 'was due 3 days ago').

The Archivo condensed page titles over DM Sans give the series a real display voice, and the Coming up numerals (big day, stacked OCT/SUN) are a lovely pairing. But Home is set small, Ideas are cards with no tabulation, and To do rows carry three lines of grey.
Same typesetting as its parent. The added glow sits on marks, not letters, so it neither helps nor hurts the type.

The best-defined scale in the heat: label .8125, small .9375, body 1.0625 (17px reading size), head 1.5 and title 3rem, with the condensed title on a hairline rule. The margin DUE timetable on To do is right-aligned tabular mono, and Status runs its detail inline after the bold name. Loses a little on Ideas: direction and duration share one centred Drive column, so 'min' never lines up.

The most careful tabulation here. Ideas splits DRIVE and WAY into their own columns so 'min' stacks exactly, the kind is an ink word in its own column, and # is right-aligned. Settings is a clean two-column name | state list, the setup steps are a one-line-per-step list at a good measure, and the condensed greeting sets tight and strong on one line. The date kicker in tracked mono caps and the small Home rows are what's left to fix.

Figures get jobs: a light condensed numeral beside each title ('Ideas 12', 'Things to do 4 open / 2 late', 'Plans 1'), bold numerals with light units in the Drive column, and big '6 working · 7 off' counts on Status. Sentence-case column heads calm the tables, and Status tabulates each name against its value. Loses on the collisions in the line-from-home labels, the right-set 'Vera' title on Chat and '2 h 5 min' losing its padded zero.

Lighting her words (mint text with a halo) softens the stems of body text on Chat, and her name, times and headings in glowing mono add noise without adding hierarchy. Otherwise the parent's typesetting, including its weaknesses (small Home rows, card Ideas).

Archivo's width axis is a clever idea (wide heads, condensed labels), but the page is crowded with tiny tracked caps (ALL PLANS, IN 4 DAYS chips), the Doto dot-matrix on the tube is hard to read at size, and three narrow Home columns set everything at 12-13px.

A real one-family system: Archivo wide for titles and the greeting, condensed 75% for labels and figures, normal for reading. The Ideas table leads with #, then kind with its icon, name at medium weight and a right-aligned BY ROAD column. Coming up is a proper timetable (date tile, title, time over relative). Marked down for the superscript numerals jammed onto the nav icons and the To do lede wrapped at a needlessly narrow measure.

The departure board with true dot leaders ('Sun 13:00 Oaks Park roller rink ……… in 4 days') is the best single typographic device in the heat, and inline nav numerals ('2 Ideas') fix the parent's badges. But To do rows stack three grey meta lines, and Home's three narrow columns keep the reading text small.

The rule is clear (Archivo for signs, Red Hat Text for sentences, Workbench on the tubes), and Workbench's raster gives the glass real CRT character. But the slashed zero reads '1Ø places', the heavy raster crowds the small tube lines, and five faces with the parent's tracked yellow caps is too many voices.

Pixelify on page titles and on item names ('Oaks Park roller rink' in pixels), with Silkscreen caps, costs legibility in the lists, and the wide pixel caps fight the reading text. The plan and to-do rows are otherwise sensibly structured.

The To do rows are well set: a mono date kicker over the bold title, right-aligned amber due words, and an '4 open  2 late  up to 100' head with a figure. The Plans list has tabular mono times. But five voices (Pixelify titles, a condensed greeting, Plex Sans, Plex Mono, Silkscreen stops), and the pixel 'Things to do' reads as a toy beside the calm body.

The clearest three-face job split in its lineage: condensed Instrument Sans display, Plex Sans for reading at 16/1.55, Plex Mono for every date and time. The Plans list's weekday kicker over a bold title with its time and To do's margin dates are good typesetting. Marked down for 'Edit, complete, or snooze' repeated as a button on every row and the 2x2 cartridges breaking names ('Oaks Park / roller rink').
The parent's typesetting unchanged (pixel item names, wide Silkscreen caps). The drawn instruments add costume around the glass but nothing to the type.

a.titles:
Best: 'What's the plan?' (track-refine, timetable-refine, pocket-refine).
- It is the family's own kitchen-table question, and short: it holds one line on a phone at 32-40px.
- The one lit word names the planner's whole job: weekends, the calendar, reminders and ideas are all 'the plan'.
- The only cost is a slight echo of the placeholder's 'Plans for the weekend', and it reads as question then answers.

Second: 'What's next for us?' (track-graft, timetable-graft, pocket-graft).
- It is warm and plural, and the lit 'next' rhymes with each lineage's NEXT UP and NOW plates, so the title and the timeline speak together.
- It narrows the job to the immediate future, though: an idea worth keeping or a wish list is not 'next'.
- The lit word sits mid-line, which sets well.

Mixed: 'What shall we line up?' (revival).
- It sets beautifully in the condensed bold on one line, and 'line up' ties to the lineage.
- 'shall we' is a touch formal.
- Lighting only 'line' splits the phrase 'line up', so the eye reads a glowing noun, not the verb. Light both words or neither.

Fails: 'What's on your mind?', carried by the dice mutants and the carried designs, says nothing of planning (the owner's complaint).

Pick 'What's the plan?' as the standard. Keep 'What's next for us?' as the alternative where a timeline hangs from the box.

a.notes: Through this lens the heat separates on four tasks. (1) Seeing what is overdue on To do. The refinements, the grafts and Desk Terminal say 'was due 3 days ago' and draw a NOW rule, while the carried designs and Typeset / Instruments still show bare dates. (2) Finding an idea again. Tables win over cards: track-refine, track-revival, track-graft and timetable-refine converted, and the Pocket lineage has not. (3) Misread numbers. Night Timetable's line numbers now read as counts or unread badges in all three of its new entrants: in the bar on Night Departures and Typeset, as superscripts on the icons in Relit. That is the lineage's most urgent fix. (4) Findability of Memory, Family and Status. Labelled bars in the track entrants, Timetable Relit and Night Departures help; Pocket Traced's phone hides them under Settings. Grafts that worked: Ideas head figures with 'Save a thought' beside 'Add an idea', To do head figures ('4 open · 2 late'), Edit buttons with words, the '6 working · 7 off' count on Status (track-graft); the Plans head sentence, the month nav beside the month name, setup shrunk to its next step, and the '+ Add an idea' row (timetable-graft); the NOW rule across To do and the quick-add (pocket-graft, once it is a real field). Grafts that did not: the numbered bar words (timetable-graft); the numbers-only 'line from home' and the unnamed lamps on the shelf (track-graft); the phone Settings menu, '1 WK/DIV' jargon and Lately added back to cards (pocket-graft). Dice mutants: Tube Lit's late words help; Typeset's Workbench and Instruments' dead knobs cost legibility and add false affordances. Removals that simplify and cost no task: 'No active reminder' on every row, the Show select replaced by keys, and setup shrunk to its next step. Worth restoring: a bell on To do rows that do have a reminder. Every candidate held focus rings, controls and sign-in well, and none failed a task outright. Measured small targets are 0 or 1 everywhere except r10-wild-3 and timetable-mut (33 of 57 on Home) and r11-wild-1 and pocket-mut (25 on To do).

scores.why: Yardstick. Every task works and the layout is familiar. But 43 of 56 Home targets are under 44px, To do shows ISO dates ('Due 2026-09-27 19:56') with no sign that anything is late, and Show is a select plus a Filter button, so 'what is overdue' takes reading and arithmetic.

Yardstick. Effortless: no small targets, every list is a table, To do shows 'was due 3 days ago' with a NOW line, the filters are latched keys, and Memory, Family and Status have words in the bar. Its only costs are a desk panel repeated on every page and a title that does not say the job.

Coming up as one line with dates and 'in 4 days' is quick to take in, and Home's To do puts its due times in the margin. But the To do page shows only raw times (no late words, no now), every row still hides its actions behind 'Edit, complete, or snooze', and Memory, Family and Status are icons with no words.

Same as its parent, but the amber lamps and a lit 'now' mark on both To do lists let you see what is overdue at a glance. The To do page still says only '27 Sep 19:56', never 'late', and the bar still hides its secondary pages behind icons.

The easiest in the heat. To do is a table (Due, Task, Who, When) with 'was due 3 days ago', a now lamp, Open/Done/Cancelled/All keys, '4 open' and a plain Edit. Ideas is a sortable-looking table with drive times. Home's To do head carries a '2 late' link, the bar has words on desktop and phone, Settings is one list with each part's state, and Status leads with what was spent. Small costs: the first setup lamp is green and reads as done, and 'Save a thought' sits among the filter tabs.

It has most of Trued's gains: a To do table with late words and keys, an Ideas table, a Status lamp legend, and 'your turn' beside the chat box. But To do's Edit is a bare pencil with no word, so a first-time parent may not find it, 'Save a thought' is a disclosure dressed as a third tab, and the 28px title's lit 'line' says the diagram, not the job.

Strong grafts that help real tasks. Ideas' head says '12 ideas · 10 on the line' with 'Save a thought' next to 'Add an idea', To do's head says '4 open · 2 late' and each row has an Edit button with the word, and Status opens with '6 working · 7 off'. Two parts cost effort: 'The line from home' is numbers only, so you have to cross-reference #7 against the table, and it pushes the list down; the Status lamp shelf's lamps have no names.

It adds real words ('3 days late', 'tomorrow 19:56') and a now stop to both To do lists, and legends on Status and To do, which helps you see what is overdue. The rest is the parent's layout: Ideas as cards, a To do form stacked above the list, icon-only secondary pages, and a 'Now Wed 00:22' readout that never ticks, so it can mislead.

Home in three columns shows everything at once, which is good. But 33 of 57 Home targets are small, the bar's numbered discs (1 Vera ... 5 Wishes) look like counts, and the yellow arrow tiles are tiny. The To do page still says 'Due 27 Sep 2026, 19:56' with an OPEN chip and no late state.

Home fits one screen at 1280 and you can see the plans, the question, To do and wishes without scrolling. Home is now in the bar, the bar has words, To do has keys with 'Was due 3 days ago' in the margin and a NOW rule, and Ideas is a table. The real misread: the superscript 1-5 on the nav icons are the standard unread-badge pattern ('Wishes ⑤' with 0 open), worst on the phone tab bar. Copper owner names also sit right beside amber late words.

It has good wording: the Plans head says '1 plan in September · next up tomorrow at 10:00', the links say 'All 4 to do' and 'All 12 ideas', there is a '+ Add an idea' row, and setup shrinks to its next step. But the bar and the phone tab bar read '2 Ideas', '4 To do', '5 Wishes' as counts (there are 12 ideas and 0 wishes), and 'Finish setting up 3' uses a number as a count right beside them. The departure board drops the calendar date, and To do rows still carry 'No active reminder' and a three-verb disclosure.

It keeps every fault of its parent (33 small Home targets, numbered discs, To do without late state) and adds Workbench on the tubes: heavy raster letters and a slashed zero that reads near an 8 in '17:00' and '$2.00'. That makes the Next up board and the radar the hardest text on the page to read at night.

The idea of time down one spine is clear, and Plans as a dated agenda is a good way to find a date. But the item names are set in a pixel face that is slow to read, 25 of 97 To do targets are small, To do shows 'SUN 27 SEP · 19:56 ... OPEN' with no late state, and the secondary icons have no words.

The pixel face is kept to page titles, and every name is now a readable sans. Home reads top to bottom as NOW (the box), NEXT, Coming up, LATER. To do has keys, '4 open 2 late', a NOW rule, a SOMEDAY lane and Edit words, and Plans' dated agenda plus the month glance makes a date easy to find. Costs: Ideas is still cards, the Month key shows an agenda, the phone's secondary pages are icons with no words, and Coming up rows are mostly empty middle.

Useful grafts. To do has a 'What needs doing…' quick-add at the top of the list, a dashed NOW rule across both To do lists, and explicit 'Edit, complete, or snooze' buttons, and Chat ends in a box marked NOW. But on the phone Memory, Family and Status are hidden under 'Settings', where nobody looks for them. The quick-add looks like a field but only opens a form, beside a second green 'Add something to do'. 'NEXT 4 WEEKS · 1 WK/DIV' is jargon, and Ideas and Lately added are back to cards.

The drawn knobs, jacks, toggle and speaker look like controls and do nothing: a false affordance a child will try to press. The heavier instruments push Coming up down about 95px, the pixel face stays on item names, and the parent's 25 small To do targets and missing late state are unchanged.

It is the family's own phrase, an open invitation to tell Vera something, it lights the word that names the job ('plan' covers weekends, outings, the calendar and reminders), and it is one short line on a phone. b.notes:
The three lineages bring the phosphor back in three different ways, and all three hold up.

- Switchboard puts the original tube back whole where the greeting is, and gives every page its own green screen.
- Console turns the glowing dots into instruments that carry numbers: ladders, jewels and a meter.
- Figure lets one live mark per drawing glow, and in To do that light runs out of the figure into the list.

For the standard, the best move would be one combined rule: one tube per page, sized to the data it reports (switchboard and figure-graft); lit marks that carry data and fade with distance or time (console-graft's ladders, figure-refine's NOW line); and matte grounded companions (bone, steel, blueprint, slate) everywhere else.

Grafted features that worked:
- console-graft: the moving-coil meter (from Desk Terminal), the jewel pilot lamp and the lamp ladders. Each is a lit instrument with a job.
- figure-graft: the round tube per page head and row-pointing that lights the figure mark. This is a true tube afterglow on real data.
- switchboard-graft: the Status lamp matrix, the lit LED on the current key and the double-height question on the glass.

Grafted features that did not work:
- switchboard-graft's mosaic pictures: matte, multicoloured and light-less. They are period teletext, but they pull the palette away from phosphor. Its emptied top bar costs the mark its place too.
- figure-graft's small Home tube: it drops the Next up words.
- console-graft's title word 'next': it doubles the NEXT UP legend.

Mutants: console-mut shows what full-strength glass looks like, and its curved corners and blip bloom should go to console-graft. Its lit window on every readout is too much glow. figure-mut's cyan links hurt the phosphor. switchboard-mut is phosphor-identical to its parent, the 'nearly identical' the owner warned about.

Glow never came across as glare in any candidate. The heaviest is switchboard-refine's Home glass (64% green share), but that green sits in one tube where attention belongs; the fix there is to calm the glass, not to put it out. The yardsticks read as I expected: today's page has all the light but spreads it, and Desk Terminal is calmer and a shade less alive than the three best here.

scores.why: Yardstick. Every effect of the original is here: the greeting lit from below through scanlines, the halo on 'mind', Send's pool, the Next up tube and the 404 radar. But the green is spread over bubbles, chips, pills and a monochrome wash, so it is the glare the owner asked to calm, not scarce light.

Yardstick. The question is typed on the glass under a block cursor, there is a moving-coil spend meter, To do has a bar tube, and lit NOW lines run through the lists. The light is calm and does jobs, but the halos are soft and Home's tube is small, so it is a little less alive than the original.

The radar tube is real and 'mind' is lit. Everywhere else it is a blueprint manual with tracked capitals and a paper-grey 'here' block. The greeting has no pool, and Status and To do show no phosphor apart from two lit ports, so it reads as a document, not a lit screen.

The light is exactly where attention belongs. The greeting is lit from the tube's side, with a tall scanlined radar, and 'plan' carries the two-layer halo. Best of all, To do's NOW line glows out of the figure and across the list itself, so the phosphor is tied to the data. Blueprint on slate keeps the rest grounded. It loses a point because Plans has no figure and no tube, and Status's spend is not a green screen.

A round phosphor tube in a blueprint instrument ring heads every page and shows that page's one live figure: $0.00 of $2.00, NEXT IN 1 DAY, READY, and an amber '2 LATE'. That is a true system of tubes, and pointing at a row lights its mark. Home's tube is small and has lost the Next up words, so the greeting's green screen says less than before.

The deeper, rounded tubes do give off more light, and the radar now blooms. But the sky-cyan links (#6ec7f1) compete with the phosphor on every row, the greeting has no pool, and small caps change nothing about the light. It is the parent's soul with a louder second colour.

It is alive: a big radar tube, a lit ask box, amber T-minus lamps and a lit annunciator. But the tracked-capital nav with square LEDs, 'CONSOLE nn' and the dashed arcs are costume, and they compete with the light instead of carrying it.

This is disciplined. The Status windows light only what is WORKING, a lit NOW needle and Next square sit on a solid track, and the ask box glows. But the readout rail is matte Plex digits and the Next up tube is shrunk to a letterbox, so Home's one green screen lost presence. Calm with less life in it.

Phosphor comes back as instruments that report data. Lamp ladders count down to each hop, a jewel pilot lamp marks what is on, the live leg of the flight plan is lit, and the moving-coil spend meter on Status is a real period green screen with bloom and scanlines. Glowing dots on the black, each with a job, while the rest is matte slate and steel.

The tube's light is restored at full strength: curved glass falling into shadow, blooming blips and the sweep's afterglow, the most original-feeling radar in the heat. But it lights every readout in its own small window, green and amber, so the glow spreads along the whole strip, and the costume (tracked caps, CONSOLE nn, zero-padding) stays.

Home's greeting is one full-strength original tube: Next up, the radar and the question typed on the glass. Each page opens on its own green summary screen, and the chat's input is a lit terminal line. That is a lot of green (55%), with brass and tracked keys around it, and 'What's on your mind?' is set as a typed prompt.

This design has the most of the original's own effect, and it sits in the right places. The greeting is a scanlined, blooming tube with 'What's the plan?' typed on it over a block-cursor well. The chat's input is a terminal line with a cursor, and every page has its own green screen (To do's bars, Plans' weekend, the spend, 'How it stands'). Around them, bone, steel and dotted leaders stay matte. It only needs calming inside the glass.

The Status lamp matrix ('every line at a glance') and the lit LED on the current key are glowing dots on black with real jobs, and the double-height question on the glass is strong. The mosaic pictures are matte multicoloured blocks that give no light and pull toward a teletext palette. The emptied top bar also costs the mark its place.
Its light is the parent's light, unchanged. Azeret's slashed zero is a nice terminal detail but invisible at a glance. Nothing new is lit, and 'What's on your mind?' stays.

Put 'Silver Falls hike' and 'tomorrow 10:00' on the tube's lower arc, or on a lit strip under it, and enlarge Home's tube to about 220px so the greeting has a real green screen. (2) Keep To do's amber phosphor tube only while something is late; otherwise use green. (3) Align the chat's sequence arrows to the thread's rows. (4) Wrap the greeting in a pool (E7) so the question is lit from the tube's side, as figure-refine does.

KEEP: the Status windows that light only WORKING, the solid violet track with a lit NOW needle and Next square on Home and Plans, and readout rails as a page system. Give its curved-glass tube, blooming blips and sweep afterglow to the lineage's best (console-graft). Do not carry over the lit window on every readout.

Either draw them in the screen green at the third strength, with one live block at full strength, or drop them from cells that have nothing live. Put the nav back in the top bar beside the mark.

b.titles: The best in this heat is 'What's the plan?' (figure-graft, console-refine, switchboard-refine, switchboard-graft). It is the family's own phrase, a real invitation to tell Vera something, and one short line on a phone. 'plan' covers the whole job (weekends, ideas, the calendar, reminders), and four letters take E1's two-layer halo well, so the key word glows cleanly. On a switchboard glass it is typed in VT323. There graft's straight apostrophe is the right typesetting call, but only 'plan' should be hot, with the rest of the line at the tube's middle strength. A close second is 'Tell Vera what to plan.' (figure-refine): the manual's imperative, naming her and the job, with a well-lit 'plan'. It is slightly stiffer, and 'what to plan' can read as if she does the planning. 'Tell Vera what's next.' (console-graft) is the weakest new title. 'next' narrows the job to what is coming (ideas worth keeping and wish lists are not 'next'). Its lit word also doubles the NEXT UP legend on the tube beside it, so two things claim the same glow. 'What's on your mind?' (carried designs and mutants) fails for the owner's reason: it says nothing of planning.

b.notes:
This heat has the most personality of any I have seen in the tour. Three lineages have found identities that reach page content rather than tint it. Figure Ground's graft gave each page one round instrument and a drawing per section. Flight Console's graft gave the plan a flown route and the spend a real needle. Switchboard's graft gave each cell a mosaic counted from its rows.

Grafts that worked:
- The round tube in a blueprint ring (figure-graft). It is the owner's lost phosphor light, brought back exactly where a figure is live.
- Amber phosphor as a second tube colour for 'late' (figure-graft's To do). It is grounded, meaningful and beautiful.
- The moving-coil meter (console-graft, from Desk Terminal). It is more memorable here than in its source, because the console gives it a home.
- The jewelled pilot lamps and the lit live leg (console-graft).
- Mosaics drawn from data (switchboard-graft, taking Figure Ground's rule into videotex terms).

Grafts that did not work, or did not land fully:
- The switchboard's bulb and gift, which are pictures, not counts.
- Console-graft's loss of the refine's leg lengths.
- Figure-graft's Home column of identical thumbnails.
- The switchboard's two key rows in rainbow caps, which is busy chrome.

Refinements:
- figure-refine's To do NOW line crossing from the figure into the list is the single best figure-to-content join in the heat. Every Figure Ground design should have it.
- console-refine is the calmest and most exact page here, but it risks the ordinary without the graft's instruments.

Mutants:
- The type mutant (Azeret) and the cyanotype mutant changed almost nothing visible, and the cyan made links worse.
- The phosphor mutant (console Aglow) is the one worth mining, for its lit readout windows and full-strength radar.

Against the yardsticks: figure-graft and console-graft both outscore Desk Terminal, Joined on this lens. They are less familiar, and their instruments come from their own metaphor. Today's page trails every lineage's best.

scores.why: Recognisably Phosphor and properly lit, but it is a stock rounded-card dark dashboard washed in one green. It is the 'Matrix' page the family named, and its structure says nothing about what is on it.

Polished and coherent: a desk-terminal rail with a tube on every page, a meter on Status, a NOW rule in To do. The mood is clear, but it is the most familiar shape here (sidebar plus list), and in this heat it is a benchmark rather than a surprise.

A genuinely new identity (an operator manual in which every section is led by a blueprint of its own data), let down by costume: 'Chapter n', tracked mono nav, a paper-grey 'here' block, raw blue-underlined links and an unlit greeting.

The manual grown up: bone ink on slate, a lit glass pool behind 'Tell Vera what to plan.', the wiring diagram with the live wire lit, the kinds figure that is also the filter, and the best single moment in the heat, To do's NOW line running out of the figure across the list. Home drops to one figure and Plans has none, so the lineage's rule is only half kept.

The most memorable system in the heat: every page head is a round phosphor tube in a blueprint instrument ring showing that page's one live figure. It reads 10:00 TOMORROW, $0.00 OF $2.00, NEXT IN 1 DAY, and on To do an amber-phosphor '2 LATE' that is lovely. The ring draws before the tube lights on power-on, and every Home section still leads with its own drawing. The Home figure column is a stack of same-size thumbnails, and the figures are small.

The rounded deep tubes are pleasant, but the cyanotype turn makes every row title stock dark-mode link blue, and small caps are still shouted caps. The page is nearly identical to its parent, faults included.

A strong metaphor with real drawings (the readout strip, dashed flight-plan arcs, the T-minus ladder, the annunciator), buried under costume: CONSOLE 03 / TARGETS OF OPPORTUNITY, HOLDS, tracked caps everywhere and padded zeros.

The costume is off and the ideas are kept. The readout rail on every page carries page-specific figures. The flight plan labels each leg with its length (3 days, 5 days, 8 days, 7 days) above violet arcs, with stops numbered to the rows, which is delightful and truly about the content. Calm and exact, but with the costume gone it drifts toward a well-made dashboard, and the Next tube is small and letterboxed.

Instruments that carry real light. The moving-coil panel meter on Status is the best single artefact in the heat. There are jewelled pilot lamps, T-minus lamp ladders beside each hop, an amber ladder down the setup steps, and a lit live leg from Now to Next. It is a complete system across Home, Plans, To do and Status. It lost the refine's leg lengths, and the Status head leaves a slab of empty slate.

The tube is switched back on well: a full-strength radar with afterglow, and the rail's figures in small lit amber and green windows like a VFD, which is worth keeping. All of the parent's costume stays, and the green share climbs.

The videotex sommaire is a fresh structure, with the question typed on the glass under a cursor. The cells stretch half-empty, brass-and-pixel-icon decoration stands in for content, and every page repeats the same boxed rack.

The most typographic entrant: contents lines with dotted leaders from name to fact, page numbers as quiet folios, 'What's the plan?' typed on the glass, and a green summary screen per page (To do's block-bar counts are charming). It is orderly and literate, but graphically it is a wall of equal boxes with coloured caps, and little on Home is drawn.

The most videotex idea yet: each cell carries a teletext mosaic counted from its own data (four weeks of calendar blocks, a clipboard of bars, family figures) under a numbered page-key row, with the question in double height on the glass. The mosaics are too small and the bulb and gift are shapes, not data. The rainbow of section caps and the double key row make the chrome busy.
Azeret Mono and a slashed zero are invisible at 12px. It is the parent unchanged in effect, with a text-wrap regression in Settings.

(6) Remove the dotted top edges on Lately added cards, which are texture noise. (7) Start the Plans month track at Now when today is late in the month, so it is not 80% empty past.

FIX: graft the moving-coil meter from the graft onto Status's cost section, and the Aglow mutant's lit readout windows (amber for Today and Late, green for counts) onto the rail. Enlarge the Next up tube: its radar and title are letterboxed in a wide low box with matte slate above and below. Give it the portrait proportion of the graft.

FIX: (1) Make every mosaic data, not a shape: Ideas as 12 blocks with the ones waiting to be looked up lit, Wishes as blocks per open wish. Drop the bulb and gift outlines. (2) Set mosaics at 80-100px on one shared baseline in each cell head, so the Home map reads as a row of pictures at a glance. (3) Quiet the chrome: the 10-key page row with coloured caps plus coloured cell caps is a rainbow. Keep colour on the current key and each cell's mosaic only, with hairline caps elsewhere. (4) Size the bottom-row cells to their content (Wishes, Family, Status, Settings carry 40-60px of empty graphite). (5) Drop Family's and Wishes' green screens. The screen should mean something is live.

KEEP the dotted-leader contents lines, the folio page numbers, the To do summary screen's block bars and the terminal as page 200. FIX: Home's glass column runs 650px tall. Tighten the Next up block so the question and the well sit higher. Take the graft's mosaics into the cell heads so Home is drawn and not only listed. The coloured section caps (lilac, sky, teal) should appear once each, not as competing tops.

If carried: keep the deep rounded tubes as the one round glowing thing on a square page, but reject the #6ec7f1 cyan links (stock dark-mode blue) and the small-caps controls. Buttons and tabs should be sentence case.

b.titles: Best: 'Tell Vera what to plan.' (t1-figure-refine). It is an invitation to tell her something, it names Vera and the whole job in one verb, the lit 'plan' is the right key word, and the manual's imperative voice makes it the lineage's own. Very close second: 'What's the plan?' (figure-graft, console-refine, both switchboard entrants). It is idiomatic, in the family's own voice and fits one line on a phone. It is at its best typed in double-height VT323 on the switchboard glass, where it reads as a terminal prompt. Its weakness is that it asks the family rather than inviting them to tell Vera, and with four designs using it, it is becoming the default rather than a lineage's own. 'Tell Vera what's next.' (console-graft) ties neatly to Next up and the ladders, but 'next' is narrower than the job: an idea to keep or a wish list is not 'next', and the lit word points at a moment, not at planning. 'What's on your mind?' (the carried designs and the mutants) fails: it is a social-media or therapist prompt that says nothing about weekends, plans, reminders or lists.

b.notes: The three refinements each became a real system that holds across pages, and all three now have zero small targets on Home. The carried designs and the mutants did not. Switchboard, Trued is the most codified: one contents line and one module-plus-register pattern everywhere. On inner pages it has converged toward Desk Terminal (the r13 yardstick), and its distinctness now lives in the Home sommaire, which is a genuinely different and useful Home. Lit Manual does the most with page content: the To do NOW line crossing the list, and the kinds chart that is the filter, are exactly what the owner means by 'reflect the page content'. It needs a figure on Plans to keep its own rule. Among the grafts, Lamps and Ladders is the one that brings the original light back tastefully. The meter, the jewelled lamps with halos and the lamp code are phosphor where something is live, and green share stays at 41%. Grafted features that WORKED: the moving-coil meter and the four-shape lamp code with its key (console-graft); the round page-head tube with one live number (figure-graft, a reusable component the Figure lineage should keep); sentence-case kind words and the 24px line (figure-graft); steel slips for the family's chat lines (console-graft, figure-graft); the calendar mosaic on Plans and clay for restaurants (switchboard). Grafted features that did NOT work: the ladder bars (they read as signal strength); the row lamp boxed beside the checkbox (control confusion); the bulb and gift mosaics and the unlabelled Status lamp matrix (switchboard-graft); the row-zero key strip as a second header; and filler figures (setup rungs, idea squares) in figure-graft. Mutants: the Cyanotype small caps do not read as small caps in the render, and its cyan makes the link fault worse. Aglow's curved glass and full radar are worth grafting into the console tubes. Retyped's mono swap is invisible at this size. Controls across the heat: the double green focus ring is consistent everywhere. The steel chosen option in selects (figure-refine) and the lit square (switchboard-graft) are both clear. Console-refine's field-focus glow is the most restrained. On the measures: the switchboards carry the most green (54-64% share) because of their panel-sized tubes, the Figure line the least (26-44%), and the Console line sits between (36-46%). The owner's 'bright where it needs to be' favours the Figure and Console lines on share. The switchboard can get there by dimming the dim-green body ink on its glass.

scores.why: Yardstick. Rounded cards and pills on every page, the Home wash in the corner, and a setup box that reads as a warning. It is lit, but it has no system beyond 'a card'. Controls and focus are fine.

A strong rule (figure column, words beside) and the best Status drawing (the wiring with lit ports). It is let down by tracked mono-cap tabs, the paper-grey 'here' slab, blue underlined row titles that look like raw HTML links, ISO due dates and 14 small targets.

A clean system: one full-width readout rail heads every page, bays sit under one top rule, steel keys carry an LED, the violet flight plan is labelled by leg length and numbered to the rows, and Status's WORKING/OFF windows carry words as well as light. It is calm and exact. The zero-padded figures (05, 00) are leftover costume, the Next up tube is small and floats in matte slate, and hue variety is thin.

The moving-coil spend meter is the best single instrument in the heat, and the jewelled lamps with halos and the four-shape lamp code (with a key on each page) are a true status system. The rail, bays and flight plan hold on every page. Against it: To do's lamp box sits beside the checkbox and reads as a second control; the ladder bars' meaning is unclear; the Home rail stops short of its bay; the figures are zero-padded; and the Status head leaves a band of empty slate.

The most codified system in the heat. One contents line (lamp, number, name, dotted leader, count) heads every Home cell and every register row. Inner pages all open on the same module (plate, one green primary, a bank of latched keys, the page's own green screen) beside a 44px register. Settings as a contents register is the best Settings in the heat, and the section-colour caps give colour a job. Faults: the whole question is set in VT323 on the glass, so 'plan' is no longer the one lit word; green share is 64%; some cells stretch empty; the steel 'today' block on the month is heavy.

But the row-zero key strip under a second top bar doubles the chrome, the bulb and gift mosaics are decoration at icon size, and the Status lamp matrix is unlabelled dots nobody can read at a glance.
The Azeret Mono swap is invisible at 12-13px, and the slashed zero is barely seen. Balanced headings help a little and 'pretty' made one break worse. All the parent's faults remain.

It is the clearest invitation, since it names who to tell and says the job in the manual's imperative voice, but it reads slightly stiff for a reminder or an idea to keep. 'Tell Vera what’s next.' (console-graft) is weaker. 'Next' narrows the job to upcoming things (ideas worth keeping and wish lists are not 'next'), and it repeats the NEXT UP legend a few centimetres away.
